name: Poland
summary_text: Detention is the clearest documented threat to a trans visitor in Poland. On 13 March 2024 the Association for Legal Intervention reported that a regional court had placed a transgender Vietnamese woman in a guarded centre for male foreign nationals. Her hormone therapy was interrupted for three months because the centre would not supply the medication, and her file recorded a history of violence and sexual assault, meaning she was held in a facility where those risks were live. She was released only after NGO intervention prompted the Border Guard commander to order it.  Trans prisoners have won on the same issue in court. On 11 July 2024 the European Court of Human Rights found that Polish prison authorities violated Article 8 of the Convention by denying a trans prisoner hormone replacement therapy, awarding EUR 8,000 in damages, while rejecting the parallel Article 3 claim. The judgment establishes that medication denial in Polish custody is litigable and can be won, though it does not prevent the denial from occurring first.  Entry rules are straightforward for short stays: Global Affairs Canada records visa-free entry for tourists staying up to 90 days, while listing sexual orientation among the reported motives for harassment in Poland, alongside physical appearance and foreigner status. The advisory therefore treats identity-based harassment as an existing condition of travel rather than a remote possibility.  Protection on paper has widened. Deputy Justice Minister Smiszek announced a hate-speech law extending protection to gender identity and sexual orientation, and a March draft amendment to the Penal Code raised penalties for anti-LGBTI hate speech and violence; it passed the Government Legislation Centre in May but the government postponed approval, with a second bill introduced in late October. The Prosecutor General established a special response team with new guidelines for law enforcement. Whether the higher penalties are in force by the time of travel is not settled in these sources.  The wider record shows an official climate that has moved in both directions. HRW's World Report 2025 describes LGBT-rights reform under the Tusk government as slow and insufficient: in June 2024 Justice Minister Bodnar revoked the Ziobro directive that had blocked recognition of same-sex marriage certificates obtained abroad, and in September the ECtHR ruled that Poland's lack of partnership recognition leaves couples in an illegal vacuum in violation of their rights, calling for a recognition framework. Earlier hostility is documented in statements and enforcement: President Andrzej Duda said in the 2020 election campaign that 'LGBT is not people, it's an ideology, which is more harmful than Communism'; municipalities and four voivodeships declared LGBT-free zones after 2015; ILGA-Europe's 2020 report ranked Poland worst among EU countries; and on 7 August 2020 some 47 people were arrested during the Rainbow Night mass arrest, drawing criticism from the Polish Ombudsman.  Public violence has been recorded at events a visitor might attend. In August 2019 LGBT community members said they felt unsafe amid rising violence, including attacks on the first Equality March in Białystok and a foiled bombing attempt at a march in Lublin. A Kalisz rally on 11 November 2021 heard its organiser describe 'LGBT, pederasts and Zionists' as enemies of Poland.

name: Paraguay
summary_text: Paraguay has no legal gender recognition procedure in force. The judiciary has yet to issue final rulings in ten lawsuits filed by trans people seeking recognition of their legal names, among them cases brought by Yren Rotela and Mariana Sepúlveda that have been pending since 2016. Both plaintiffs have taken communications to the UN Human Rights Committee under the Optional Protocol to the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights and are awaiting a decision. Trans people are not allowed to change their name and gender on official documents, so a trans visitor whose passport marker conflicts with their presentation has no domestic route to alignment.  Amnesty International's 2025-26 report records two trans migrants who were denied identity documents, evidence that the documentary gap reaches administrative encounters rather than staying theoretical.  There is no general anti-discrimination law covering gender identity or sexual orientation, and no hate-crime statute is recorded in the sources. A November 2015 bill to ban discrimination on those grounds has not advanced since its introduction. Protections that do exist are narrow and sector-specific, addressing sexual orientation in dormitory placement, violence against women, stateless persons, personal data and the internal staffing rules of one public office. None supplies a general remedy to a trans visitor refused service, accommodation or police assistance.  Violence and discrimination against LGBT people remain frequent in Paraguay and are often ignored by the police. An Associated Press report of September 2025 found that discrimination, harassment and gender-based violence push trans women out of their hometowns and into migration and sex work, a pattern that shapes the settings a trans visitor may move through.  Official hostility is documented at national and municipal level alike. The government banned discussion of LGBT issues in public schools in October 2017, and the Minister of Education said he might consider burning books that raise awareness about transgender people. Asunción's city council banned an event honouring a trans human-rights defender who died in March, per Amnesty International. Horacio Cartes, a senior ruling-party figure, said in 2017 that he would "shoot himself in the testicles" if his son married another man, later apologising to those offended.  Same-sex marriage and civil unions are not recognised in Paraguayan law. The Inter-American Court of Human Rights has held in an advisory opinion that OAS signatories must allow same-sex marriage; Paraguay is an OAS party and is bound by the ruling, while domestic law has not been brought into line. A trans visitor's partner therefore has no standing under local law.  Same-sex sexual activity has been legal in Paraguay since 1990. The sources record an age of consent of 16 for homosexual conduct and 14 for heterosexual conduct.  Healthcare carries one trans-specific entitlement. Resolution 695, approved by the Ministry of Public Health and Social Welfare in October 2016, requires that health service officials record and treat transgender patients under their identified social name on medical records, medical histories and forms. Law 7018 on Mental Health, enacted 15 November 2022, states that a mental health diagnosis cannot be made on the exclusive basis of sexual choice or identity.

sources.title: Constitution of Paraguay (1992), Articles 49, 50, 51, 52
sources.documents: Limits marriage, de facto unions and family to 'one man and one woman'; basis for non-recognition of same-sex couples.
sources.detail: Cited as Article 49 'Protection of the Family', Article 50 'Right To Constitute a Family', Article 51 'Legal Marriages and the Effects of De Facto Unions', Article 52 'Union in Marriage' - in force since 1992
